<reason>Both sides debated well and narrowed the clash cleanly. B (PRO) won a real sub-clash on privacy: the "next of kin" objection was squarely answered by pointing out intestacy is a default that yields to a will, and A effectively dropped that line afterwards. B also landed a legitimate hit that A's DRM-free/mandated-transferability world is a larger intervention and is not the motion. But A built the more decisive comparative. A's rivalry framing forced B into the "one seat" design, and A then exploited that concession relentlessly: a seat is unsplittable and, crucially, unsaleable, so probate's usual "divide value, not things" answer fails for the one asset class B has chosen; B's late reply that the statute would "create the conditions for" a market was handwaving. A's A1/A2 answers were the sharpest speech of the debate: transferability changes the thing (rivalrous chattel that passes automatically), while the motion changes only the timing and thereby entrenches the license permanently. Most damaging of all, B volunteered that "the heir's claim dies with the entity," and A converted that into the closing frame — a guarantee whose content is the seller's continued goodwill. B's counterparty-risk analogy softened but did not neutralize it, and B's charge that A "leaves platform licensing untouched" misdescribed A's stated remedies. Two clipped B turns are a modest execution cost. A's shorter closing crystallized the choice better than B's, which partly recycled the counterparty-risk line.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answer to B's "probate divides value, not things": A distinguished indivisible-but-saleable assets (piano, ring, house) from the motion's uniquely unsaleable seat, so losing heirs get nothing rather than a share of value — combined with A's exploitation of B's own admission that "the heir's claim dies with the entity."</best_rebuttal>
